documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations
documents.content:
Extra binary formats to register with the kernel, each mapping a way of recognising a binary onto the interpreter which should run it.
Note that nixos' {option}boot.binfmt.emulatedSystems has no counterpart here: it is a convenience which derives qemu registrations from a list of systems, and deriving them is the part this module leaves to whoever wants it. A qemu interpreter named here works exactly as any other does.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.fixBinary
documents.content: Open the interpreter at registration time and hold it open, so that the format keeps working inside a mount namespace which cannot see the interpreter's path (the F flag).

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.interpreter
documents.content:
The interpreter to hand a matching binary to.
Reached through /run/binfmt/‹name› rather than directly: the kernel's field for this is 127 bytes, which a store path does not reliably fit in.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.magicOrExtension
documents.content:
The magic sequence to match, or the filename extension (without its dot).
Written to the kernel as given, so the escapes the kernel understands - \x for a byte, \\ for a backslash - are the escapes to use.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.mask
documents.content: A mask applied to the candidate bytes before comparing them with {option}magicOrExtension, so that a field which varies can be ignored. null means every byte must match.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.matchCredentials
documents.content: Launch the interpreter with the credentials the binary would have had, setuid bits included (the C flag). Implies {option}openBinary.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.offset
documents.content: The byte offset of the magic sequence. Meaningless for an extension.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.openBinary
documents.content: Open the binary and pass the descriptor to the interpreter rather than its path (the O flag). Implied by {option}matchCredentials.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.preserveArgvZero
documents.content: Pass the original argv[0] to the interpreter (the P flag).

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.recognitionType
documents.content: Whether to recognise the binary by a magic sequence or by a filename extension.

documents.title: Option: boot.binfmt.registrations.<name>.wrapInterpreterInShell
documents.content: Whether to wrap {option}interpreter in a shell script. Needed when it is itself a script, since the kernel will not run one binfmt interpreter through another. Turn it off for a real ELF binary, and for {option}fixBinary, which needs something openable.

documents.title: Option: boot.deviceAliases
documents.content:
Groups of names which refer to the same block device.
A machine names its root however it likes - /dev/disk/by-uuid/... is what a NixOS hardware scan writes, and what most configurations carry. The kernel cannot use that: it reads root= before any userspace exists, and those paths are symlinks udev or mdevd make once they are running. Telling this module which names mean the same device lets it hand the kernel one it can resolve, instead of refusing the configuration.
Each element is one device under all of its names. nixos-facter reports exactly that, as unix_device_names on each entry under hardware.disk:
Nothing here depends on facter - a group written by hand does as well, and lsblk -o NAME,PATH,PARTUUID,UUID is where the names come from either way.
Only consulted when there is no initrd and the root is named as something the kernel cannot resolve. A machine with an initrd resolves its own root in stage 1, as it always has.

documents.title: Option: boot.init
documents.content:
Executable run as stage-2 PID 1, symlinked as ${config.system.build.toplevel}/init.
Set from {option}providers.services.backend, which names the init and the supervisor in one choice. This module deliberately has no default: naming one implementation here made it PID 1 whatever the contract said, which is the coupling the contract exists to remove.

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.availableKernelModules
documents.content: The set of kernel modules in the initial ramdisk used during the boot process. This set must include all modules necessary for mounting the root device. That is, it should include modules for the physical device (e.g., SCSI drivers) and for the file system (e.g., ext3). The set specified here is automatically closed under the module dependency relation, i.e., all dependencies of the modules list here are included automatically. The modules listed here are available in the initrd, but are only loaded on demand (e.g., the ext3 module is loaded automatically when an ext3 filesystem is mounted, and modules for PCI devices are loaded when they match the PCI ID of a device in your system). To force a module to be loaded, include it in {option}boot.initrd.kernelModules.

documents.content:

documents.title: Option: boot.initrd.finit.services.<name>.exec-reload
documents.content:
Some services do not support SIGHUP but may have other ways to update the configuration of a running daemon. When exec-reload is defined it is preferred over SIGHUP. Like systemd, finit sets ``$MAINPIDas a convenience to scripts, which in effect also allow settingexec-reload` to `kill -HUP $MAINPID`.
::: {.note} exec-reload is called as PID 1, without any timeout! Meaning, it is up to you to ensure the script is not blocking for seconds at a time or never terminates. :::

documents.title: Option: boot.kernel.builtinDrivers
documents.content:
Kernel modules to build into the kernel rather than leave as modules, named the way the kernel names them: nvme, ahci, sd_mod, mmc_block, usb_storage, virtio_blk.
The other half of reaching a root without an initrd. Knowing the filesystem is no use if nothing in the kernel can talk to the disk it is on, and the kernel nixpkgs builds leaves NVMe and MMC as modules - so on most modern hardware, where the root is an NVMe disk, {option}boot.kernel.builtinFilesystems alone is not enough.
Named after the modules because that is what everything which knows the answer already produces. lsmod says nvme; so does nixos-facter, whose report gives each storage controller a driver_modules and which feeds exactly that list to {option}boot.initrd.availableKernelModules on a machine which has an initrd. A machine with a report can hand the same list to this:
A module this has no configuration for is an assertion rather than a silent omission, which is the point of naming them rather than deriving them: a machine whose disk hangs off something unusual is told so while it can still be fixed, instead of booting to a kernel which cannot see it.
Defaulted to all of them rather than to whichever this machine needs, because a configuration does not reliably say which that is: a root named by label or by uuid, which is how most machines name their disks, says nothing about what it is on. Building all of them in costs nothing over building one, since a machine without an initrd is having a kernel built for it either way.
Set this to [ ] to build none of them, on a machine which has some other reason to believe its kernel can reach its disk.

documents.title: Option: boot.kernel.builtinFilesystems
documents.content:
Filesystems to build into the kernel rather than leave as modules, named the way {option}fileSystems.<name>.fsType names them.
Defaulted from the machine's own root filesystem, because on a machine with no initrd that is precisely the one the kernel has to be able to mount unaided - so a btrfs root needs no second statement that the kernel should understand btrfs.
Derived whether or not the kernel appears to build it in already, which is not a question worth asking: the answer is different per architecture - on x86_64 ext4, vfat, squashfs and 9p are all modules, on aarch64 none of them are - and a machine without an initrd is building a kernel regardless, since the storage drivers go into it.
Setting this replaces the default rather than adding to it.
What this is for is a root the kernel has to reach unaided. A module cannot be loaded before the filesystem holding it is mounted, so an initrd exists to carry the driver for the root across that gap - and a kernel which already has the driver needs no initrd at all. See {option}boot.initrd.enable.
Only needed for a filesystem the kernel does not already build in: the stock pkgs.linuxPackages has ext4, 9p, squashfs and virtio among others, and adding one of those here asks for a kernel build which changes nothing.
Anything this option has not heard of is named directly in {option}boot.kernel.structuredExtraConfig.

documents.title: Option: boot.kernel.randstructSeed
documents.content: Provides a custom seed for the {var}RANDSTRUCT security option of the Linux kernel. Note that {var}RANDSTRUCT is only enabled in NixOS hardened kernels. Using a custom seed requires building the kernel and dependent packages locally, since this customization happens at build time.

documents.title: Option: boot.kernel.structuredExtraConfig
documents.content:
Kernel configuration symbols to set, in the form {manpage}Kconfig(5) names them and with the values lib.kernel builds - yes, module, no, freeform, option.
The escape hatch behind {option}boot.kernel.builtinFilesystems, and the way to build in anything else: whatever is set here is merged over what the filesystem names resolved to, so it also overrides them.
Setting either means building the kernel, which is not a small thing to ask for. A machine which can boot with a stock kernel should.

documents.title: Option: boot.kernelPackages
documents.content:
This option allows you to override the Linux kernel used by NixOS. Since things like external kernel module packages are tied to the kernel you're using, it also overrides those. This option is a function that takes Nixpkgs as an argument (as a convenience), and returns an attribute set containing at the very least an attribute {var}kernel. Additional attributes may be needed depending on your configuration. For instance, if you use the NVIDIA X driver, then it also needs to contain an attribute {var}nvidia_x11.
Please note that we strictly support kernel versions that are maintained by the Linux developers only. More information on the availability of kernel versions is documented in the Linux section of the manual.

Environment variables to set for POSIX-compliant login shells (bash, zsh, dash, ...) via {file}/etc/profile.d/. Shells with non-POSIX syntax, such as fish, do not source these scripts and will not pick up these variables.
The value of each variable can be a string, a path, an integer, or a list of those, in which case the list is joined with :.
Setting a variable to null does not set anything on its own, but lets you override a value set by another module to effectively cancel it out.

documents.title: Option: fileSystems
documents.content:
The file systems to be mounted. It must include an entry for the root directory (mountPoint = "/"). Each entry in the list is an attribute set with the following fields: mountPoint, device, fsType (a file system type recognised by {command}mount; defaults to "auto"), and options (the mount options passed to {command}mount using the {option}-o flag; defaults to [ "defaults" ]).
Instead of specifying device, you can also specify a volume label (label) for file systems that support it, such as ext2/ext3 (see {command}mke2fs -L).

documents.title: Option: fileSystems.<name>.depends
documents.content: List of paths that should be mounted before this one. This filesystem's {option}device and {option}mountPoint are always checked and do not need to be included explicitly. If a path is added to this list, any other filesystem whose mount point is a parent of the path will be mounted before this filesystem. The paths do not need to actually be the {option}mountPoint of some other filesystem.

Signal finit sends to reload the service, or "none" when the service does not handle SIGHUP and must be stopped and started on reconfiguration instead.
See upstream documentation for details.

documents.title: Option: finit.sysv.<name>.reload-triggers
documents.content: An arbitrary list of items such as derivations. If any item in the list changes between reconfigurations, the service will be reloaded or restarted if reloads are not supported.

documents.title: Option: finit.sysv.<name>.respawn
documents.content: Enable endless restarts without counting toward the retry limit. When set, the service will be restarted indefinitely regardless of the restart-max limit.

documents.title: Option: finit.sysv.<name>.restart-max
documents.content: The number of times finit tries to restart a crashing service. When this limit is reached the service is marked crashed and must be restarted manually with initctl restart NAME. When null, finit's built-in default applies.

documents.title: Option: finit.sysv.<name>.restart-sec
documents.content: The number of seconds before Finit tries to restart a crashing service, default: 2 seconds for the first five retries, then back-off to 5 seconds. The maximum of this configured value and the above (2 and 5) will be used.

documents.title: Option: finit.sysv.<name>.rlimit
documents.content:
An attribute set of resource limits that will be apply by finit.
See upstream documentation for additional details.

documents.title: Option: finit.sysv.<name>.runlevel
documents.content: See upstream documentation for details.

documents.title: Option: finit.sysv.<name>.runtime-dir
documents.content:
A directory name, resolved under /run, created before the service starts and owned by its user and group. Absolute paths and .. are refused. The resolved path is exported to the process environment as $RUNTIME_DIRECTORY.
Removed again when the service stops, after any exec-stop-post script has run, unless runtime-dir-preserve says otherwise.
See upstream documentation for additional details.

documents.title: Option: finit.sysv.<name>.runtime-dir-mode
documents.content: The mode of runtime-dir, locked down again on every start, default: 0755. Modes are octal, with the leading zero.

documents.title: Option: finit.sysv.<name>.runtime-dir-preserve
documents.content:
Whether runtime-dir survives the service stopping, the same values as systemd's RuntimeDirectoryPreserve=, default: false.
false - removed when the service stops
"restart" - kept across restarts, removed on a real stop
true - never removed

documents.title: Option: finit.sysv.<name>.state-dir

documents.title: Option: finit.sysv.<name>.state-dir-mode

documents.title: Option: finit.sysv.<name>.stop-timeout

documents.title: Option: finit.sysv.<name>.user

documents.title: Option: finit.tasks.<name>.cache-dir

documents.title: Option: finit.tasks.<name>.conditions

documents.title: Option: finit.tasks.<name>.config-dir

documents.title: Option: finit.tasks.<name>.config-dir-mode

documents.content:

With remain-after-exit, the task runs once and does not re-run on runlevel. The exec-stop-post script will run if the task is explicitly stopped or when the task leaves its valid runlevels.

documents.title: Option: finit.tmpfiles.clean.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable automatic cleaning of temporary files.
:::{.note} You must have a scheduler backend configured with providers.scheduler.backend to utilize this option. :::

documents.title: Option: finit.tmpfiles.clean.interval
documents.content:
The interval at which this task should run its specified {option}command. Accepts either a standard {manpage}crontab(5) expression or one of: hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, or yearly.
If a standard {manpage}crontab(5) expression is provided this value will be passed directly to the scheduler implementation and execute exactly as specified.
If one of the special values, hourly, daily, monthly, weekly, or yearly, is provided then the underlying scheduler implementation will use its features to decide when best to run.

documents.title: Option: finit.tmpfiles.rules
documents.content:
Rules for creation, deletion and cleaning of volatile and temporary files automatically. See {manpage}tmpfiles.d(5) for the exact format.
Only read when finit is the selected backend, because reading them at all is a thing finit can do and the other implementations cannot - it ships a {manpage}tmpfiles.d(5) parser, and dinit, runit and s6 do not. Anything which should work under any init belongs in {option}providers.services.tmpfiles.rules, which is declared as attrsets lowered into commands at build time and so needs no parser at all.

documents.title: Option: finit.ttys.<name>.baud

documents.title: Option: finit.ttys.<name>.command
documents.content: Specify an external getty, like agetty or the BusyBox getty.

documents.title: Option: finit.ttys.<name>.conditions
documents.content: See upstream documentation for details.

documents.title: Option: finit.ttys.<name>.device
documents.content: Embedded systems may want to enable automatic device by supplying the special @console device. This works regardless weather the system uses ttyS0, ttyAMA0, ttyMXC0, or anything else. finit figures it out by querying sysfs: /sys/class/tty/console/active.

documents.title: Option: finit.ttys.<name>.enable

documents.title: Option: finit.ttys.<name>.noclear
documents.content: Disables clearing the TTY after each session. Clearing the TTY when a user logs out is usually preferable.

documents.title: Option: finit.ttys.<name>.nologin
documents.content: Disables getty and /bin/login, and gives the user a root (login) shell on the given TTY device immediately. Needless to say, this is a rather insecure option, but can be very useful for developer builds, during board bringup, or similar.

documents.title: Option: finit.ttys.<name>.notty
documents.content: No device node mode. This is insecure and intended only for board bringup or testing scenarios.

documents.title: Option: finit.ttys.<name>.nowait
documents.content: Disables the press Enter to activate console message before actually starting the getty program.

documents.title: Option: finit.ttys.<name>.reload-triggers

documents.title: Option: finit.ttys.<name>.rescue

documents.title: Option: finit.ttys.<name>.term

documents.title: Option: fonts.enableDefaultPackages
documents.content: Enable a basic set of fonts providing several styles and families and reasonable coverage of Unicode.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.allowBitmaps
documents.content: Allow bitmap fonts. Set to false to ban all bitmap fonts.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.allowType1
documents.content: Allow Type-1 fonts. Default is false because of poor rendering.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.antialias
documents.content: Enable font antialiasing. At high resolution (> 200 DPI), antialiasing has no visible effect; users of such displays may want to disable this option.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.cache32Bit
documents.content: Generate system fonts cache for 32-bit applications.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.defaultFonts.emoji
documents.content:
System-wide default emoji font(s). Multiple fonts may be listed in case a font does not support all emoji.
Note that fontconfig matches color emoji fonts preferentially, so if you want to use a black and white font while having a color font installed (eg. Noto Color Emoji installed alongside Noto Emoji), fontconfig will still choose the color font even when it is later in the list.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.defaultFonts.monospace
documents.content: System-wide default monospace font(s). Multiple fonts may be listed in case multiple languages must be supported.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.defaultFonts.sansSerif
documents.content: System-wide default sans serif font(s). Multiple fonts may be listed in case multiple languages must be supported.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.defaultFonts.serif
documents.content: System-wide default serif font(s). Multiple fonts may be listed in case multiple languages must be supported.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.enable
documents.content: If enabled, a Fontconfig configuration file will be built pointing to a set of default fonts. If you don't care about running X11 applications or any other program that uses Fontconfig, you can leave this option off and prevent a dependency on all those fonts.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.hinting.autohint
documents.content: Enable the autohinter in place of the default interpreter. The results are usually lower quality than correctly-hinted fonts, but better than unhinted fonts.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.hinting.enable
documents.content: Enable font hinting. Hinting aligns glyphs to pixel boundaries to improve rendering sharpness at low resolution. At high resolution (> 200 dpi) hinting will do nothing (at best); users of such displays may want to disable this option.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.hinting.style
documents.content:
Hintstyle is the amount of font reshaping done to line up to the grid.
slight will make the font more fuzzy to line up to the grid but will be better in retaining font shape, while full will be a crisp font that aligns well to the pixel grid but will lose a greater amount of font shape.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.includeUserConf
documents.content: Include the user configuration from {file}~/.config/fontconfig/fonts.conf or {file}~/.config/fontconfig/conf.d.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.localConf
documents.content: System-wide customization file contents, has higher priority than defaultFonts settings.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.subpixel.lcdfilter
documents.content: FreeType LCD filter. At high resolution (> 200 DPI), LCD filtering has no visible effect; users of such displays may want to select none.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.subpixel.rgba
documents.content: Subpixel order. The overwhelming majority of displays are rgb in their normal orientation. Select vrgb for mounting such a display 90 degrees clockwise from its normal orientation or vbgr for mounting 90 degrees counter-clockwise. Select bgr in the unlikely event of mounting 180 degrees from the normal orientation. Reverse these directions in the improbable event that the display's native subpixel order is bgr.

documents.title: Option: fonts.fontconfig.useEmbeddedBitmaps
documents.content: Use embedded bitmaps in fonts like Calibri.

Such files will be loaded automatically if the kernel asks for them (i.e., when it has detected specific hardware that requires firmware to function). If multiple packages contain firmware files with the same name, the first package in the list takes precedence. Note that you must rebuild your system if you add files to any of these directories.

documents.title: Option: hardware.graphics.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable hardware accelerated graphics drivers.
This is required to allow most graphical applications and environments to use hardware rendering, video encode/decode acceleration, etc.
This option should be enabled by default by the corresponding modules, so you do not usually have to set it yourself.

documents.title: Option: hardware.graphics.enable32Bit
documents.content: On 64-bit systems, whether to also install 32-bit drivers for 32-bit applications (such as Wine).

documents.title: Option: hardware.graphics.extraPackages
documents.content:
Additional packages to add to the default graphics driver lookup path. This can be used to add OpenCL drivers, VA-API/VDPAU drivers, etc.
::: {.note} intel-media-driver supports hardware Broadwell (2014) or newer. Older hardware should use the mostly unmaintained intel-vaapi-driver driver. :::

documents.title: Option: hardware.graphics.extraPackages32
documents.content:
Additional packages to add to 32-bit graphics driver lookup path on 64-bit systems. Used when {option}enable32Bit is set. This can be used to add OpenCL drivers, VA-API/VDPAU drivers, etc.
::: {.note} intel-media-driver supports hardware Broadwell (2014) or newer. Older hardware should use the mostly unmaintained intel-vaapi-driver driver. :::

documents.title: Option: hardware.i2c.enable

documents.title: Option: hardware.i2c.group
documents.content:
Group to own the /dev/i2c-* devices.
::: {.note} If you want non-root users to be able to access these i2c devices, add them to this group. :::
::: {.note} If left as the default value this group will automatically be created on system activation, otherwise you are responsible for ensuring the group exists before system activation has completed. :::

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable NVIDIA driver support.

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.gsp.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable the GPU System Processor (GSP) on the video card.

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.kernelModule
documents.content: Which NVIDIA kernel module to use: the "open" source GPU kernel modules (recommended on Turing and later GPUs, required on the newest GPUs) or the "closed" proprietary ones.

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.modesetting.enable
documents.content:
Whether to enable kernel modesetting when using the NVIDIA proprietary driver.
Enabling this can fix screen tearing. This is not enabled by default because it is not officially supported by NVIDIA and would not work with SLI.
Enabling this and using version 545 or newer of the proprietary NVIDIA driver causes it to provide its own framebuffer device, which can cause Wayland compositors to work when they otherwise wouldn't.

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.package
documents.content: The NVIDIA driver package to use.

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.power.runtime.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable fine-grained dynamic power management. When enabled, the NVIDIA GPU is powered down when not in use. Only works in PRIME offload mode (prime.offload.enable = true). Requires kernel >= 5.5 and a Turing or newer GPU. Sets NVreg_DynamicPowerManagement=0x02.

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.power.suspend.enable
documents.content: Whether to preserve video memory allocations across system suspend and hibernate. For more information, see the NVIDIA docs, on Chapter 21. Configuring Power Management Support.

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.power.suspend.notifier
documents.content:
How the NVIDIA driver is notified of system suspend and resume events when power.suspend.enable is set:
kernel: the kernel notifies the driver directly. Requires NVIDIA driver version 595 or newer, and the open source kernel modules.
userspace: relies on nvidia-sleep.sh being run by the sleep backend (requires a sleep backend, e.g. programs.zzz).

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.prime.amdgpuBusId
documents.content: The PCI bus ID of the AMD iGPU (for AMD+NVIDIA Optimus laptops). Find it with: lspci | grep -i amd | grep -i vga

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.prime.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable nvidia PRIME support.

documents.title: Option: hardware.nvidia.reduceTearing
documents.content:
Reduce screen tearing on displays connected directly to the NVIDIA GPU by enabling its full composition pipeline. This sets the ForceFullCompositionPipeline metamode and, alongside it, disables indirect GLX and enables triple buffering on the X screen.
Trade-offs: it forces the screen to be redrawn even when nothing changed, which can reduce the performance of OpenGL/fullscreen applications (and has been reported to cause issues with WebGL), and it increases the time the driver takes to clock down after load.
See https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/NVIDIA/Troubleshooting#Avoid_screen_tearing_on_Xorg.

documents.title: Option: nixpkgs.hostPlatform
documents.content:
The platform this machine runs on.
A fact about the machine rather than about the package set, which is what lets it be checked: when a package set is also handed in, an assertion compares the two rather than trusting that whoever built it chose the same answer.
To cross-compile, set {option}nixpkgs.buildPlatform as well.

documents.title: Option: nixpkgs.overlays

A module needing a package nixpkgs does not have - or a different build of one it does - says so here, rather than the caller having to know what every module on the machine will want. Unlike the options above these apply either way: to a set built here, and to one handed in through {option}nixpkgs.pkgs, where they are appended after whatever it already carries.

Setting this makes {option}nixpkgs.config, {option}nixpkgs.hostPlatform and {option}nixpkgs.buildPlatform inert: they describe how to build a package set, and this one is already built. {option}nixpkgs.overlays still apply, because a built set can be extended.

NixOS reads the tree it is itself part of; finix is not part of one and pins none, so whoever evaluates a machine says which nixpkgs it is evaluated against. Needed only when {option}nixpkgs.pkgs is not set.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.agentPKCS11Whitelist
documents.content:
A pattern limiting which PKCS#11 or FIDO libraries ssh-add -s may load into the agent, as ssh-agent -P takes it. Null leaves ssh-agent's own default, which permits nothing but its compiled-in paths.
Not needed for a FIDO token through ssh-add -K: that goes through the agent's built-in security-key support rather than a loaded provider.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.agentTimeout
documents.content: How long the agent keeps a key before forgetting it, as ssh-agent -t takes it, or null to keep keys until the session ends.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.askPassword
documents.content:
A program which prompts for a passphrase or a token's PIN, exported as {env}SSH_ASKPASS, or null to leave it unset.
Only reached when there is no terminal to ask on. ssh prompts on the tty whenever it has one - the test is isatty(stdin), not whether a display is set - so somebody running ssh-add in a terminal never gets here, on X11 or Wayland or neither.
What does get here is a prompt with stdin redirected: a unit, a hook, an editor's git integration, anything run without a controlling terminal. With this null such a prompt cannot be answered at all, because the openssh package ships no askpass of its own and the compiled-in default does not exist:
{env}SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE is the other half of this and is left to the environment: force uses the program even when there is a tty, never refuses it even when there is not.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.enable
documents.content:
Whether to install the ssh client and write the system-wide {file}/etc/ssh/ssh_config and {file}/etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts.
This is the client. The server is {option}services.openssh.enable.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.extraConfig
documents.content: Lines placed at the top of {file}/etc/ssh/ssh_config, before the generated Host * block - which is what makes them override it. ssh takes the first value it finds for an option, so anything after that block cannot change it.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.knownHosts
documents.content:
The system-wide known hosts, written to {file}/etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts.
Knowing a host's key ahead of time is what makes the first connection to it meaningful: without it ssh asks, and a script answering that question is answering it blind.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.knownHosts.<name>.certAuthority
documents.content: Whether this key is an ssh certificate authority rather than one host's key.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.knownHosts.<name>.extraHostNames
documents.content: Further names and addresses, added to the default {option}hostNames. Ignored when that is set explicitly.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.knownHosts.<name>.hostNames
documents.content: The names and addresses this key is accepted for. The attribute's own name is in here by default; setting this explicitly drops that, and {option}extraHostNames adds to it without dropping it.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.knownHosts.<name>.publicKey
documents.content: The key itself: a type and a key, with no host names in front of it - ssh-keyscan prints them with, so the names have to come off.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.knownHosts.<name>.publicKeyFile
documents.content: A file holding that same thing, read at build time. One key only; a host with several wants an entry each, or {option}programs.ssh.knownHostsFiles.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.knownHostsFiles
documents.content: Further known-hosts files, named in GlobalKnownHostsFile after {file}/etc/ssh/ssh_known_hosts. For a host with several keys, where {option}knownHosts takes one each.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.package
documents.content: The package to use for ssh.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.settings
documents.content:
ssh_config(5) options, written into the Host * block. A bool becomes yes/no, a list becomes the comma-separated form those options take, and null drops the key.
Per-host blocks go in {option}extraConfig, since a Host pattern is structure rather than a key and a value.

documents.title: Option: programs.ssh.startAgent
documents.content:
Whether to run ssh-agent in each normal user's session.
The agent listens on {file}$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/ssh-agent and {env}SSH_AUTH_SOCK is exported into the session, so everything started by it - including a terminal which proxies the agent onward - finds the same one.
One agent per session rather than per user, which is what this contract can express: the tree is started by the session and stops with it, so the keys do not outlive a logout. That is the behaviour wanted from an agent holding a hardware token.
Independent of {option}programs.ssh.enable, which is about the client's configuration file; this is about a daemon.

documents.title: Option: providers.resumeAndSuspend.hooks.<name>.event

documents.title: Option: providers.scheduler.backend
documents.content: The selected module which should implement functionality for the {option}providers.scheduler contract.

documents.title: Option: providers.scheduler.supportedFeatures.user
documents.content: Whether the selected {option}providers.scheduler implementation supports running tasks as a specified user.

documents.title: Option: providers.scheduler.tasks
documents.content: A set of tasks which are to be run at specified intervals.

documents.title: Option: providers.scheduler.tasks.<name>.command
documents.content: The command this task should execute at specified {option}intervals.

documents.title: Option: providers.scheduler.tasks.<name>.interval
documents.content:
The interval at which this task should run its specified {option}command. Accepts either a standard {manpage}crontab(5) expression or one of: hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, or yearly.
If a standard {manpage}crontab(5) expression is provided this value will be passed directly to the scheduler implementation and execute exactly as specified.
If one of the special values, hourly, daily, monthly, weekly, or yearly, is provided then the underlying scheduler implementation will use its features to decide when best to run.

documents.title: Option: providers.scheduler.tasks.<name>.user
documents.content: The user this task should run as, subject to {option}provider.scheduler implementation capabilities. See {option}providers.scheduler.supportedFeatures and your selected backend implementation for additional details.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.backend
documents.content:
The selected module which should implement functionality for the {option}providers.services contract.
This is PID 1 as well as the supervisor: the module named here points {option}boot.init at its own executable. The two are not separable, because an init is not only a thing which supervises units - it is also what the kernel hands the machine to. An implementation which cannot be that is not selectable here.
It rarely needs saying directly: every implementation sets this from its own enable, so dinit.enable = true is the whole of selecting dinit. Each does so as a default, which is what leaves this option able to override the choice, and what makes enabling two of them a conflict rather than one of them quietly winning.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.ctl.enable
documents.content:
Whether to install initctl, the front-end over every implementation's units, where the implementation can support it.
Turning it off leaves initctl to whatever else provides one - on finit that is finit's own, which talks only to the system tree - and each implementation's tool reachable under its own name.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.initPaths.<name>.copy
documents.content: A copy of a tree, replacing whatever is there, made after activation.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.initPaths.<name>.copy.from
documents.content: The tree to copy. Symlinks in it are followed: it is in the store, and a copy of store links would be read-only whatever writable said.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.initPaths.<name>.copy.writable
documents.content: Whether the copy is made writable by its owner.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.initPaths.<name>.directory
documents.content: A directory, created after activation.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.initPaths.<name>.fifo
documents.content: A named pipe, made after activation - which a derivation cannot contain.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.initPaths.<name>.fifo.mode
documents.content: The pipe's permissions, as a number: 384 is 0600.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.initPaths.<name>.mount
documents.content: A filesystem, mounted before activation.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.initPaths.<name>.mount.device
documents.content: What to pass as the source. A pseudo-filesystem ignores it, but mount still wants one, and it is what shows up in findmnt.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.initPaths.<name>.mount.fsType
documents.content: The filesystem type, as the kernel names it.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.initPaths.<name>.mount.options
documents.content: Mount options, split by finix-init into flags and data the way every other mount here is.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.initPaths.<name>.symlink
documents.content: A symbolic link, made after activation.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.initPaths.<name>.symlink.target
documents.content: What the link points at. An existing link is replaced.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.mountFilesystems
documents.content:
Whether to mount the filesystems in {option}fileSystems which the initrd did not, as the mount-filesystems unit at the head of the trunk.
An implementation which mounts them itself before any unit runs - finit reads /etc/fstab as part of being finit - can turn this off, though leaving it on is harmless: mount -a skips what is already mounted.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.runit.serviceDir
documents.content:
The generated runit service directories.
runsv creates a supervise directory inside each service directory, so this cannot be scanned out of the store: it must be copied somewhere writable first, and the copy must not be repeated while runsvdir is running, or the tree is deleted out from under it.
Hosting is left to the system rather than done here, because runit is not an init and has to be supervised by whatever is. See tests/providers/services-runit.nix for the arrangement under finit:
a task which copies this somewhere writable, exactly once
a service running runsvdir over that copy, with runit on its PATH, since runsvdir execs runsv by name

documents.title: Option: providers.services.s6-rc.database
documents.content:
The compiled service database.
s6-rc runs against a database rather than a directory of configuration, so this is built rather than written out - a malformed unit fails the build instead of the boot.
Hosting is the system's business, as s6-rc supervises under whatever is PID 1: s6-svscan over a scan directory, then s6-rc-init -c <this>/db -l /run/s6-rc against it. See tests/providers/services-s6rc.nix.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.supportedFeatures.group
documents.content: Whether the selected {option}providers.services implementation can run a unit under a given group.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.supportedFeatures.path
documents.content: Whether the selected {option}providers.services implementation can give a unit its own PATH. Where it cannot, a unit's command must name everything it runs absolutely.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.supportedFeatures.readiness
documents.content:
Every readiness kind the selected {option}providers.services implementation can observe, named as it is tagged in {option}providers.services.units.<name>.type.
A kind absent from this list cannot be honoured, and asking for one is refused.
This lists the whole vocabulary rather than only the protocols needing the daemon's cooperation, because the ones that do not are not universally available either. waitFor.pidfile says the daemon forks and the process which was spawned exits; runsv and s6-supervise read that exit as a crash and restart it forever, so on those two it cannot work at all - where finit and dinit both watch it natively. Listing only notify and s6 left that unsayable, and so unrefused.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.supportedFeatures.startTimeout
documents.content:
Whether the selected {option}providers.services implementation can bound how long a unit may take to become ready before it is considered failed.
When false, a unit which never becomes ready stalls every unit which requires it, directly or transitively, for the remainder of the boot.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.supportedFeatures.stopTimeout
documents.content: Whether the selected {option}providers.services implementation can bound how long a unit may take to stop before it is killed outright.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.supportedFeatures.user
documents.content: Whether the selected {option}providers.services implementation can run a unit as a given user. An implementation which cannot must say so, since the alternative is running as root something which asked not to be.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.switch.activate
documents.content:
A program reading unit names on standard input, one per line, and starting them.
Names arrive in dependency order, so acting on them in the order given starts each unit after everything it requires. An implementation which reconciles from its own configuration may ignore the names entirely and simply reload.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.switch.deactivate
documents.content:
A program reading unit names on standard input, one per line, and stopping them.
No order is specified, and none is needed: dependencies gate starting only, so nothing is ever waiting for another unit to stop.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.switch.list
documents.content:
A program printing every unit the implementation currently has active, one per line, as a name and a fingerprint separated by a tab.
The fingerprint is the one the implementation was given when the unit was written, and is only ever compared for equality - it is opaque to the implementation and means nothing to it.
An implementation which reconciles from its own configuration may print nothing. Every unit is then reported as new, {option}activate is handed the whole tree, and that implementation's own reconciliation does the work.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules
documents.content:
Volatile files and directories to put in place during early boot, as the tmpfiles-setup unit at the head of the trunk - so everything attached to any later trunk level is behind them.
Rules are attrsets rather than {manpage}tmpfiles.d(5) lines because they are lowered into commands when the system is built. Nothing on the machine parses them, so an implementation needs no reader of that format to be selectable as a backend - which matters for dinit, runit and s6, none of which ship one.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.path
documents.content:
The absolute path the rule applies to.
Taken literally, not as a pattern - except for a remove rule, where shell glob characters match and a pattern matching nothing is not an error.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type
documents.content:
What the rule does, and whatever that needs.
directory and file create the path if it is not already there. symlink points it at {option}argument, which that kind alone requires. permissions creates nothing and only changes a path which already exists, for something another unit or the kernel has made. remove deletes it, and is the one kind whose {option}path may be a glob.
A kind carrying nothing beyond path may be written as a bare string, so type = "remove" and type.remove = { } mean the same thing.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type.directory
documents.content: Create the path as a directory if it is not there yet.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type.directory.group
documents.content: Owning group, by name or numeric id. null leaves it alone.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type.directory.mode
documents.content: Access mode, as {manpage}chmod(1) would take it. null leaves it alone - for a path being created, that means the process umask decides.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type.directory.user
documents.content: Owning user, by name or numeric id. null leaves ownership with whoever created the path, which this early in boot is root.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type.file
documents.content: Create the path as a file if it is not there yet.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type.file.argument
documents.content: Initial contents. null creates an empty file.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type.file.group
documents.content: Owning group, by name or numeric id. null leaves it alone.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type.file.mode
documents.content: Access mode, as {manpage}chmod(1) would take it. null leaves it alone - for a path being created, that means the process umask decides.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type.file.user
documents.content: Owning user, by name or numeric id. null leaves ownership with whoever created the path, which this early in boot is root.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type.permissions
documents.content: Change ownership and/or mode on a path which already exists; creates nothing.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type.permissions.group
documents.content: Owning group, by name or numeric id. null leaves it alone.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type.permissions.mode
documents.content: Access mode, as {manpage}chmod(1) would take it. null leaves it alone - for a path being created, that means the process umask decides.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type.permissions.recursive
documents.content: Whether the rule descends into the path's contents. permissions then applies to everything beneath the path; remove otherwise refuses a non-empty directory.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type.permissions.user
documents.content: Owning user, by name or numeric id. null leaves ownership with whoever created the path, which this early in boot is root.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type.remove
documents.content: Delete the path.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type.remove.recursive
documents.content: Whether the rule descends into the path's contents. permissions then applies to everything beneath the path; remove otherwise refuses a non-empty directory.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type.symlink
documents.content: Point the path at {option}argument as a symlink.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.tmpfiles.rules.*.type.symlink.argument
documents.content: The link's target.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.trunk.latch
documents.content:
The one level which does not resolve during normal operation.
Everything before it is the boot sequence. The latch itself is reached only once every unit before it has stopped, which only happens when the system is going down - so everything after it is the shutdown sequence, ordered by the same chain, and a unit which needs to run on the way out attaches to a level after the latch rather than needing a concept of its own.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.trunk.levels
documents.content:
The trunk, in order. Each entry becomes an anchor unit requiring the previous level and everything attached to it.
A level is named for the tier it marks the completion of, not the tier which attaches to it: units attached to sysinit are the basic tier, and once they are up, basic is reached. So the first level exists only to be attached to - start marks nothing, because nothing has happened yet - and the last boot level, running, marks the whole userspace being up and has nothing attached to it.
Levels at or after {option}latch are the shutdown sequence: they cannot be reached while the system is running, so units attached to them run on the way down.
::: {.note} A level becomes a unit name in the selected backend, so it must not collide with a name that backend reserves. boot is unusable for this reason: it is dinit's own root service, and a trunk level of that name would overwrite it. :::

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units
documents.content:
The system's service graph.
A unit starts when, and only when, every unit it requires has become ready. There is no other mechanism for starting one: no runlevels, no enablement, no activation events. A unit which requires nothing starts immediately, because its requirements are trivially met.
Dependencies govern starting only. Once a unit is running it is unaffected by what happens to the units it required - if one of them stops, crashes, or restarts, this unit keeps running. Nothing in the graph stops anything; units are only ever stopped by shutdown or by reconfiguration.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.description
documents.content: A short human-readable description of this unit.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.enable
documents.content:
Whether this unit is part of the system.
A disabled unit is not emitted at all, and is stopped on the next reconciliation if it happens to be running. Units which require it are left waiting, since the thing they require will never become ready - so disabling a unit something else depends on is a way to stall that branch of the graph, not a way to prune it.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.environment
documents.content: Environment variables passed to this unit's process.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.group
documents.content: The group this unit runs as.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.path
documents.content:
Packages and directories placed on this unit's PATH.
Units are given a deliberately bare environment, so anything invoking a program by name rather than by store path needs to say where to find it.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.reloadTriggers
documents.content:
Files this unit's process reads which are not named anywhere else in the unit, listed so that changing one counts as changing the unit.
A unit's identity is what {option}providers.services.switch compares across a rebuild: the command, the user, the environment, and the rest of what is written here. A daemon which reads a configuration file from a fixed path - /etc/elogind/logind.conf, say - names it nowhere, so the file can change while every one of those stays identical, and the daemon keeps running with the configuration it started with. Nothing reports it.
Naming the file here makes it part of the unit, so the switch acts on it. What it does is reload where it can: a changed unit which declares {option}type.service.reload is asked to re-read its own configuration and keeps its pid, and only one which cannot is stopped and started. Hence the name - a restart is the fallback, not the intent. Whether reloading is enough is the unit's claim to make, which is why it is made there.
Only for what the unit does not otherwise mention. A path which already appears in the command - as an argument, or in a generated script - is part of the unit by being there, and needs no second statement.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.requires
documents.content:
The units which must be ready before this one starts. Losing one afterwards has no effect on this unit.
At most one of these may be a trunk level - see {option}providers.services.trunk.levels.
A unit which requires nothing is attached to the first trunk level instead of floating free, so that it still has a place in the tree and the second level still waits for it. Setting this to an empty list explicitly opts out.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.restartIfChanged
documents.content:
Whether a switch may stop and start this unit when its definition has changed.
True for almost everything: a changed unit is one whose new definition is not what is running, and the point of a switch is to make the machine match the generation. Set false where applying the change costs more than leaving it pending, and the new definition then takes effect the next time the unit starts for any other reason.
What that is for is a unit whose restart destroys something the user did not ask to lose. A display manager is the case: restarting it ends every session on the machine, so a switch which touched it would log the user out - and if the switch is being run from one of those sessions, it takes the rest of the switch with it. That is not hypothetical; it is how a generation comes to be activated and never recorded, because the tool driving it was killed between the two halves.
Unrelated to being added or removed. A unit that is genuinely new is still started and one that is gone is still stopped - this says only that changing it is not reason enough to interrupt it.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.startTimeout
documents.content: How long, in seconds, this unit may take to become ready before it is considered failed. Subject to {option}providers.services.supportedFeatures.startTimeout.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.stopTimeout
documents.content:
How long, in seconds, this unit is given to exit after being asked to stop, before it is killed outright. Subject to {option}providers.services.supportedFeatures.stopTimeout.
Implementation defaults are chosen for units which exit promptly and are usually only a few seconds. Anything which flushes state on the way out - a database especially - should say so here rather than be killed mid-write.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.terminal
documents.content:
Whether this unit's command opens a terminal itself and makes it its standard input, output and error - a getty, or a greeter run through one. An implementation must then leave the unit's output alone rather than capture it.
Capturing is not merely pointless for such a program, it is harmful. finit's log forks a logger as a child of the unit's own process; the getty points its output at the terminal, the logger exits, and the unit is left holding a child it never made. login is then exec'd into that process, forks the shell, and waits for any child - reaping the logger instead, concluding the session is over, and exiting, at which point the kernel hangs up the shell before it has run a line. Every login on the machine returns straight to the prompt with nothing printed. tests/getty-login.nix pins it.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.type
documents.content:
What kind of unit this is, and whatever that kind needs.
service is a long-running process. oneshot is a command which runs to completion and is ready once it has exited successfully. anchor has no process at all and is ready once its own requirements are.
Anchors exist to be named, so a unit can say "after the system is basically up" without naming the units that means. In practice they are the trunk, and ordinary modules have no reason to declare one - an interchangeable implementation should be selected by a providers. contract and define the shared unit name directly, rather than hiding behind an anchor.
A kind carrying nothing may be written as a bare string, so type = "anchor" and type = { anchor = { }; } mean the same thing.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.type.anchor
documents.content: A unit with no process at all.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.type.oneshot
documents.content: A command which runs to completion.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.type.oneshot.command
documents.content:
The command this unit runs.
May be left out when {option}readiness is set, for a unit whose only job is to wait for something - a device node appearing, say - so that whatever requires it waits too.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.type.oneshot.readiness
documents.content:
Something which must be live, after the command has exited, before this unit counts as done.
Without it a oneshot is ready the moment its command exits successfully. With it, it is ready once the command has exited and the thing named here has appeared, and units requiring it wait for both. Every waitFor kind is accepted, and works on every implementation: the wait is run as part of the unit's own command, so nothing has to observe it.
Only waitFor: fork, notify and s6 describe a process which stays running, and a oneshot is one which does not.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.type.oneshot.readiness.waitFor
documents.content:
Ready once something appears and is live, for a daemon with no readiness protocol of its own - which is most of them.

documents.content:

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.type.oneshot.readiness.waitFor.check.command
documents.content: The command whose successful exit means ready.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.type.oneshot.readiness.waitFor.path
documents.content: Ready once the path exists, which is all that can be known about an arbitrary file.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.type.oneshot.readiness.waitFor.path.path
documents.content: The path to wait for.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.type.oneshot.readiness.waitFor.pidfile
documents.content:

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.type.oneshot.readiness.waitFor.pidfile.file
documents.content: The file the daemon writes its process ID to.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.type.oneshot.readiness.waitFor.socket
documents.content:

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.type.oneshot.readiness.waitFor.socket.path
documents.content: The socket this unit binds.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.type.oneshot.readinessTimeout
documents.content:
How long, in seconds, the wait in {option}readiness may take before the unit fails. Its dependants then never start, and the rest of the boot carries on without them.
null waits indefinitely - which, for something that may never appear, holds everything behind this unit for as long as the machine is up. Unlike {option}startTimeout this is enforced by the unit itself, so it works on every implementation.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.type.service
documents.content: A long-running process.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.type.service.command
documents.content: The command this unit runs.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.type.service.readiness
documents.content:
How this unit reports that it has become ready, and so how units requiring it learn they may start.
There are two sorts here, and the difference is who decides.
notify and s6 are the daemon saying so - an sd_notify READY=1 on the notification socket, or an s6 notification on a descriptor. Both need the program's cooperation, so an implementation may not be able to observe them and will refuse them rather than downgrade.

That works with a program which cannot report anything, which is most of them, and every implementation can do it - by its own mechanism where it has one, by polling otherwise. It is inference rather than assertion: a unix socket's path exists from bind, which is fractionally before listen.
fork treats the unit as ready the moment it has been forked. That is a lie for anything doing real startup work, and is worth reaching for only when nothing appears that could be waited on.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.type.service.reload
documents.content:
A command which makes this daemon re-read its configuration, if it can.
Setting it declares the unit reloadable, and a switch then reloads it where it would otherwise have stopped and started it. That is the module author's judgement, not something which can be worked out here: it says this daemon picks up everything about its own definition that is allowed to change without being restarted.
The command is run directly rather than asked of the supervisor. Most are self-contained - keyd reload, nzbget --reload - and the ones which need to signal a running process can find it themselves; asking each implementation for a reload verb would mean four different ones, and dinit and runit would be reduced to sending a bare signal anyway.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.units.<name>.user
documents.content: The user this unit runs as.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.user.backend
documents.content:

It need not be the implementation running the system, and usually is not: the system's is PID 1 and cannot also be one user's, so this names whichever one can serve that scope. Every user tree is then supervised by an instance of it started by that user's session.
There is no default. An implementation which cannot run as a user leaves {option}providers.services.user.manager at none, and naming {option}providers.services.users without an implementation that can is refused - see the assertion there.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.user.manager.none
documents.content: This implementation cannot supervise a user's tree. It is the default, so an implementation says this by saying nothing - which is the safe way round: a new backend that has not thought about the user scope offers no user services, rather than offering a broken one.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.user.manager.supervisor
documents.content: This implementation has a per-user mode and can be one user's own supervisor.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.user.manager.supervisor.command
documents.content:
Given a username, the argv which supervises that user's units - the program and its arguments, executed directly. There is no shell, so a value here is never interpreted: a redirection or a pipe among these would be a literal argument.
It is run by {option}providers.services.user.sessionLauncher, as the user, inside their session - so it inherits that session's environment, and must not daemonise away from it.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.user.manager.supervisor.stop
documents.content:
Given a username, a command which stops that user's supervisor - run as the user when the session ends, in place of signalling.
Null, the default, means {option}stopSignal is enough. Set this where the process the launcher owns is not the supervisor and so cannot be asked: systemd is the case, where a systemd --user is a unit of pid 1's and the launcher's child is the systemctl start --wait which asked for it. Signalling that client says nothing about the job it enqueued; systemctl stop is the only thing that does.
The launcher still waits for its own child afterwards, and still escalates to SIGKILL - so a stop which stops nothing is bounded rather than a session which never ends.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.user.manager.supervisor.stopSignal
documents.content:
The signal which asks this implementation's supervisor to stop supervising, sent by {option}providers.services.user.sessionLauncher to the process it started when the session ends.
TERM for almost everything, and HUP for runit, where the difference is not cosmetic: runsvdir on TERM "exits with 0 immediately" and leaves every runsv it was monitoring running, so the session would end, the supervisor would exit cleanly, and the whole tree would stay - which from the outside is indistinguishable from a correct teardown.
The launcher escalates to SIGKILL if the process is still there five seconds later, whatever this is.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.user.sessionCommand
documents.content:
What a session entry - a .desktop file in share/wayland-sessions or share/xsessions - puts in its Exec=, so that a module providing a session never has to know whether there are user trees, or what starts the bus:
payload is an argv. sessionEnv and log are {option}providers.services.user.sessionLauncher's --session-env and --log, and are left out of the command when null.
With {option}providers.services.users declared this is the session launcher around the payload. Without, it is the payload under dbus-run-session, and sessionEnv and log are unused - there is no tree to tell and no relay to run.
An X session passes no sessionEnv: the display manager starts the server and sets DISPLAY before it runs Exec=, so the tree inherits it like everything else.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.user.sessionLauncher
documents.content:
What a login session runs instead of running its payload directly:
It starts a session bus when {option}services.dbus.enable is set and the session does not already have one, starts the payload, runs --session-env until it succeeds, exports what that printed, starts that user's supervisor with it, and stops the supervisor and then the bus when the payload exits. The payload's exit status is its own.
The bus listens on a socket in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR under a name the daemon chooses, and its address reaches the session the way everything else here does, by inheritance - so no session needs dbus-run-session around it.
--user defaults to the user the launcher runs as, so that one session entry can serve everyone a greeter offers it to.
--log relays the payload's, the supervisor's and the bus's output to syslog under that tag, with colour stripped, rather than leaving it on the terminal the session was given.
--session-env is the only compositor-specific part of a graphical session, and is supplied by the caller so that nothing here needs to know what a wayland socket is called. Succeeding means the session is usable; what it prints, as one NAME=VALUE per line, is what the session has to tell the tree about itself - WAYLAND_DISPLAY, whose value the compositor chose after it started and which therefore cannot be inherited.
A program, executed with no arguments, rather than a command for a shell to evaluate - as is every other command this runs. A caller with something to say in shell says it in a script, which is what one that had a shell command was already passing: a store path is one word either way.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.user.waylandSessionEnv
documents.content:
A --session-env for any wayland compositor which binds a wayland-N socket in $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR: it succeeds once there is one, printing WAYLAND_DISPLAY.
It takes the lowest-numbered socket, so it is only right while the user has one graphical session.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.users
documents.content:
Per-user service trees, one per user.
A user's units are written as if that user were the only thing on the machine, and are the only things they may depend on: the supervisor running them is that user's own and cannot observe the system's units, so an edge naming one is refused rather than silently never satisfied. Anything a tree needs from the system belongs earlier in the trunk, where it is up before any session can start.
These start with a session and stop with it, which is what separates them from a system unit that merely runs as a user - {option}providers.services.units with user set is still the way to say that.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.users.<name>.sessionVariables
documents.content:

Set before the payload, so that what a compositor spawns inherits them. {option}providers.services.user.sessionLauncherEnv is for the other case, a value only knowable once the session is running.
A value may refer to other variables, so one can extend itself the way environment.d(5) allows: $XDG_CONFIG_DIRS, ${XDG_CONFIG_DIRS}, ${XDG_CONFIG_DIRS:+:$XDG_CONFIG_DIRS} and the :- form all do what they look like, resolved against the session's environment and against the variables set before this one.
Those four forms are the whole of it. The launcher substitutes them itself and has no shell, so a value containing a command substitution is the text it is written as rather than a command that runs - which is the one way the shell this replaced could have been made to do something. A $ that begins none of the four is a literal $, and there is no way to write one that would.

Not merely that the path is there: a unix socket exists from bind, and listen comes afterwards, so a client arriving in that window is refused by a socket which demonstrably exists.

documents.content: The socket this unit binds.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.users.<name>.units.<name>.type.oneshot.readinessTimeout
documents.content:
How long, in seconds, the wait in {option}readiness may take before the unit fails. Its dependants then never start, and the rest of the boot carries on without them.
null waits indefinitely - which, for something that may never appear, holds everything behind this unit for as long as the machine is up. Unlike {option}startTimeout this is enforced by the unit itself, so it works on every implementation.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.users.<name>.units.<name>.type.service.command

documents.title: Option: providers.services.users.<name>.units.<name>.type.service.readiness
documents.content:
How this unit reports that it has become ready, and so how units requiring it learn they may start.
There are two sorts here, and the difference is who decides.
notify and s6 are the daemon saying so - an sd_notify READY=1 on the notification socket, or an s6 notification on a descriptor. Both need the program's cooperation, so an implementation may not be able to observe them and will refuse them rather than downgrade.
waitFor is the supervisor inferring it from something appearing: a pid file, a socket, any path. That works with a program which cannot report anything, which is most of them, and every implementation can do it - by its own mechanism where it has one, by polling otherwise. It is inference rather than assertion: a unix socket's path exists from bind, which is fractionally before listen.
fork treats the unit as ready the moment it has been forked. That is a lie for anything doing real startup work, and is worth reaching for only when nothing appears that could be waited on.

documents.title: Option: providers.services.users.<name>.units.<name>.type.service.reload
documents.content:
A command which makes this daemon re-read its configuration, if it can.
Setting it declares the unit reloadable, and a switch then reloads it where it would otherwise have stopped and started it. That is the module author's judgement, not something which can be worked out here: it says this daemon picks up everything about its own definition that is allowed to change without being restarted.
The command is run directly rather than asked of the supervisor. Most are self-contained - keyd reload, nzbget --reload - and the ones which need to signal a running process can find it themselves; asking each implementation for a reload verb would mean four different ones, and dinit and runit would be reduced to sending a bare signal anyway.
null for a daemon with no such command, which is then restarted.

The getty's command line is its own syntax, and the contract cannot know it. autologin is a user name or null; a getty which cannot log anyone in without a prompt should throw when it is set.

You can use {command}nix-instantiate --eval --strict '<nixpkgs/nixos>' -A config.nix.settings to view the current value. By default it is empty.

As with {option}nix.settings.trusted-users, you can specify groups by prefixing them with @. Also, you can allow all users by specifying *. The default is *. Note that trusted users are always allowed to connect.

documents.title: Option: services.nix-daemon.settings.auto-optimise-store
documents.content: If set to true, Nix automatically detects files in the store that have identical contents, and replaces them with hard links to a single copy. This saves disk space. If set to false (the default), you can still run nix-store --optimise to get rid of duplicate files.

documents.title: Option: services.nix-daemon.settings.cores
documents.content: This option defines the maximum number of concurrent tasks during one build. It affects, e.g., -j option for make. The special value 0 means that the builder should use all available CPU cores in the system. Some builds may become non-deterministic with this option; use with care! Packages will only be affected if enableParallelBuilding is set for them.

documents.title: Option: services.nix-daemon.settings.max-jobs
documents.content: This option defines the maximum number of jobs that Nix will try to build in parallel. The default is auto, which means it will use all available logical cores. It is recommend to set it to the total number of logical cores in your system (e.g., 16 for two CPUs with 4 cores each and hyper-threading).

documents.title: Option: services.nix-daemon.settings.require-sigs
documents.content: If enabled (the default), Nix will only download binaries from binary caches if they are cryptographically signed with any of the keys listed in {option}nix.settings.trusted-public-keys. If disabled, signatures are neither required nor checked, so it's strongly recommended that you use only trustworthy caches and https to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks.

documents.title: Option: services.nix-daemon.settings.sandbox
documents.content:
If set, Nix will perform builds in a sandboxed environment that it will set up automatically for each build. This prevents impurities in builds by disallowing access to dependencies outside of the Nix store by using network and mount namespaces in a chroot environment.
This is enabled by default even though it has a possible performance impact due to the initial setup time of a sandbox for each build. It doesn't affect derivation hashes, so changing this option will not trigger a rebuild of packages.
When set to "relaxed", this option permits derivations that set __noChroot = true; to run outside of the sandboxed environment. Exercise caution when using this mode of operation! It is intended to be a quick hack when building with packages that are not easily setup to be built reproducibly.

documents.title: Option: services.nix-daemon.settings.substituters

By default https://cache.nixos.org/ is added.

documents.title: Option: services.nix-daemon.settings.trusted-public-keys
