documents.title: Option: swapDevices.*.label
documents.content: Label of the swap device (if any).

documents.title: Option: swapDevices.*.options
documents.content: Options used to set up the swap device.

documents.title: Option: swapDevices.*.priority
documents.content: Specify the priority of the swap device. Higher numbers indicate higher priority. null lets the kernel choose a priority, starting at -1 and going down.

documents.title: Option: swapDevices.*.randomEncryption.allowDiscards
documents.content: Whether to allow TRIM requests to the underlying device. This option has security implications, see the upstream NixOS manual section on swap encryption.

documents.title: Option: swapDevices.*.randomEncryption.cipher
documents.content: Specify the cipher to use, see {command}cryptsetup benchmark for a list of options.

documents.title: Option: swapDevices.*.randomEncryption.enable
documents.content: Encrypt swap device with a random key. This way you won't have a persistent swap device, the entire contents become unreadable after every reboot. Mutually exclusive with {option}label, since the underlying mapped device is regenerated on every boot and is therefore not activated through /etc/fstab like a regular swap device, but through a dedicated finit task.

documents.title: Option: swapDevices.*.randomEncryption.keySize
documents.content: Specify the size of the randomly generated key, in bits.

documents.title: Option: swapDevices.*.randomEncryption.sectorSize
documents.content: Specify the sector size in bytes, or 0 to let {command}cryptsetup pick the default.

documents.title: Option: swapDevices.*.randomEncryption.source
documents.content: Source of randomness used to generate the swap encryption key on every boot.

documents.title: Option: system.activation.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable system activation scripts.

documents.title: Option: system.activation.out
documents.content: the actual script to run on activation....

documents.title: Option: system.activation.path
documents.content: Packages added to the PATH environment variable of activation scripts.

documents.title: Option: system.activation.scripts
documents.content: A set of shell script fragments that are executed when a NixOS system configuration is activated. Examples are updating /etc, creating accounts, and so on. Since these are executed every time you boot the system or run {command}nixos-rebuild, it's important that they are idempotent and fast.

documents.title: Option: system.activation.scripts.<name>.deps
documents.content: List of dependencies. The script will run after these.

documents.title: Option: system.activation.scripts.<name>.text
documents.content: The content of the script.

documents.title: Option: system.switch.inhibitors
documents.content: Attribute set of strings that will prevent switching into a configuration when they change. The switch can be manually forced on the command line if required.

documents.title: Option: system.topLevel
documents.content: top-level system derivation

documents.title: Option: systemd.enable
documents.content:
Whether to boot systemd as PID 1, supervising this configuration's {option}providers.services units.
It supervises those and nothing else. finix keeps eudev, elogind, dbus, the syslog daemon and the tmpfiles provider, and systemd's own versions of each are not installed - so this is the narrower of the two ways to run systemd here, and the one which leaves the rest of finix alone.
Enabling it points {option}providers.services.backend at systemd, which is what actually selects an implementation - so this is a default, and a machine naming a backend directly still wins.

documents.title: Option: systemd.package
documents.content:
The systemd to boot, and to drive with systemctl.
Only some of its binaries are installed - see the comment on {option}environment.systemPackages in this module. The package as a whole would collide with eudev's udevadm, elogind's loginctl and the systemd-tmpfiles shim nixos-compat installs.

documents.title: Option: systemd.standardOutput
documents.content:
What StandardOutput= and StandardError= a generated unit gets.
kmsg rather than systemd's own default of journal, because this backend runs no journald: a unit's output would be handed to a socket which does not exist and discarded. The kernel ring buffer is where finix's shutdown sequence already reports itself, and dmesg reads it back.
The cost is the kernel's printk rate limit, which a chatty daemon will reach. Set null to discard output on a machine where that matters more, or any other value {manpage}systemd.exec(5) accepts.

documents.title: Option: systemd.userSupervisor.enable
documents.content:
Whether a systemd --user, started by each user's session, supervises that user's units.
Enabling it points {option}providers.services.user.backend at systemd, which is what actually selects an implementation for that scope - so this is a default, and a machine naming a backend directly still wins.
Requires {option}systemd.enable, because this module arranges the user scope out of pid 1 systemd - the /run/systemd/system marker systemd --user looks for, and the delegated cgroup its manager unit is given - and {option}services.polkit.enable, because that manager is a system unit their session has to ask pid 1 to start. Both are asserted; see the messages there for what each would take to lift.

documents.title: Option: time.timeZone
documents.content: The time zone used when displaying times and dates. See https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones for a list of valid time zone names.

documents.title: Option: users.defaultUserShell
documents.content: The default shell assigned to user accounts created with {option}isNormalUser = true.

documents.title: Option: users.groups
documents.content: This option has no description.

documents.title: Option: users.groups.<name>.gid
documents.content: The group GID. If the GID is null, a free GID is picked on activation.

documents.title: Option: users.groups.<name>.members
documents.content: The user names of the group members, added to the /etc/group file.

documents.title: Option: users.groups.<name>.name
documents.content: The name of the group. If undefined, the name of the attribute set will be used.

documents.title: Option: users.users
documents.content: This option has no description.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.createHome
documents.content: Whether to create the home directory and ensure ownership as well as permissions to match the user.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.description
documents.content: A short description of the user account, typically the user's full name. This is actually the “GECOS” or “comment” field in {file}/etc/passwd.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.enable
documents.content: If set to false, the user account will not be created. This is useful for when you wish to conditionally disable user accounts.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.extraGroups
documents.content: The user's auxiliary groups.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.group
documents.content: The user's primary group.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.home
documents.content: The user's home directory.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.isNormalUser
documents.content: Indicates whether this is an account for a “real” user. This automatically sets {option}group to users, {option}createHome to true, {option}home to {file}/home/«username», {option}shell to {option}users.defaultUserShell, and {option}isSystemUser to false. Exactly one of isNormalUser and isSystemUser must be true.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.isSystemUser
documents.content: Indicates if the user is a system user or not. This option only has an effect if {option}uid is {option}null, in which case it determines whether the user's UID is allocated in the range for system users (below 1000) or in the range for normal users (starting at 1000). Exactly one of isNormalUser and isSystemUser must be true.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.name
documents.content: The name of the user account. If undefined, the name of the attribute set will be used.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.packages
documents.content: The set of packages that should be made available to the user. This is in contrast to {option}environment.systemPackages, which adds packages to all users.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.password
documents.content: Specifies the hashed password for the user.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.passwordFile
documents.content: The full path to a file that contains the hash of the user's password. The password file is read on each system activation. The file should contain exactly one line, which should be the password in an encrypted form that is suitable for the chpasswd -e command.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.shell
documents.content: The path to the user's shell. Can use shell derivations, like pkgs.bashInteractive. Don't forget to enable your shell in programs if necessary, like programs.zsh.enable = true;.

documents.title: Option: users.users.<name>.uid
documents.content: The account UID. If the UID is null, a free UID is picked on activation.

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.android.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable Android container support (Waydroid).

documents.title: Option: virtualisation.vmVariant
documents.content:
Configuration to add to the machine when it is built as a virtual machine, and to no other build of it.
The place to put whatever a machine needs in order to be worth running in qemu but has no business carrying on real hardware - more memory, a mount the test wants to exist, a service turned off because the hardware it drives is not there:

documents.title: Option: xdg.autostart.enable
documents.content: Whether to install files to support the XDG Autostart specification.

documents.title: Option: xdg.icons.enable
documents.content:
Whether to install files to support the XDG Icon Theme specification.
This is what puts /share/icons on {option}environment.pathsToLink, so a machine with it off has profiles containing no icon themes at all, whatever was installed into them - a per-user profile is a buildEnv over that list, not a view of the packages. Anything resolving an icon by name, which on a desktop is most things, then finds nothing.

documents.title: Option: xdg.icons.fallbackCursorThemes
documents.content: Names of the fallback cursor themes, in order of preference, to be used when no other icon source can be found. Empty disables the fallback entirely.

documents.title: Option: xdg.mime.addedAssociations
documents.content: Adds associations between mimetypes and applications. See the specifications for more information.

documents.title: Option: xdg.mime.defaultApplications
documents.content: Sets the default applications for given mimetypes. See the specifications for more information.

documents.title: Option: xdg.mime.enable
documents.content: Whether to install files to support the XDG Shared MIME-info specification and the XDG MIME Applications specification.

documents.title: Option: xdg.mime.removedAssociations
documents.content: Removes associations between mimetypes and applications. See the specifications for more information.

documents.title: Option: xdg.portal.config
documents.content:
Which backend implements which portal interface, as {manpage}portals.conf(5).
Installing a backend says it exists; this says when to use it. With one backend the question does not arise - with two that implement the same interface, xdg-desktop-portal picks between them by a rule nobody wants to depend on, so it has to be told.
Each attribute becomes a file under {file}/etc/xdg/xdg-desktop-portal: common becomes {file}portals.conf, and any other name becomes {file}<name>-portals.conf, matched against XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP.

documents.title: Option: xdg.portal.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable XDG desktop portals.

documents.title: Option: xdg.portal.package
documents.content: The package to use for xdg-desktop-portal.

documents.title: Option: xdg.portal.portals
documents.content: List of XDG desktop portal packages to install.

documents.title: Option: xdg.sounds.enable
documents.content: Whether to install files to support the XDG Sound Theme specification.

documents.title: Option: xdg.terminal-exec.enable
documents.content: Whether to enable xdg-terminal-exec, the proposed Default Terminal Execution Specification.

documents.title: Option: xdg.terminal-exec.package
documents.content: The xdg-terminal-exec package to use.

documents.title: Option: xdg.terminal-exec.settings
documents.content:
Configuration options for the Default Terminal Execution Specification.
The keys are the desktop environments that are matched (case-insensitively) against $XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP, or default which is used when the current desktop environment is not found in the configuration. The values are a list of terminals' desktop file IDs to try in order of decreasing priority.
